2022_27_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_a.paragraph: Troy School District's Annual Comprehensive Financial Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2022 came before the Board of Education as agenda item 8.B on October 18, 2022, carrying an unmodified opinion from Plante & Moran dated October 5, 2022. Governmental activities ended the year with a net position deficit of $(178,223,715) after a change in net position of $22,834,243, attributed primarily to the net decrease in deferred pension and OPEB costs. Combined governmental fund balance was $50,654,086, including a General Fund balance of $32,980,837 in what the district calls its seventh consecutive year of adding to fund balance.
2022_27_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_a.page:
**What it is**
Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) with supplemental information for Troy School District, a school district in the State of Michigan, for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2022. Prepared by the Department of Business Services at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, and transmitted October 5, 2022 by Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, and Kandice Moynihan, Director of Finance. Auditor: Plante & Moran, unmodified opinion dated October 5, 2022. No findings or questioned costs for federal awards. ASBO International has awarded the district a Certificate of Excellence for fiscal years ended June 30, 1989 through 2021.

**Government-wide position, June 30, 2022**

| Line | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Total assets | $275,756,255 |
| Total deferred outflows of resources | $65,093,678 |
| Total liabilities | $382,908,130 |
| Net pension liability | $210,869,230 |
| Net OPEB liability | $13,509,781 |
| Total deferred inflows of resources | $136,165,518 |
| Net investment in capital assets | $82,106,682 |
| Unrestricted | $(266,630,339) |
| Total net position (deficit) | $(178,223,715) |

Governmental-activity expenses totaled $187,017,923 against charges for services of $4,858,412 and operating grants and contributions of $60,219,352. General revenue of $144,774,402 included $35,621,090 of property taxes levied for general purposes, $17,683,639 for debt service, $4,214,109 for capital projects, and $82,313,714 of unrestricted state aid. Change in net position was $22,834,243, from a beginning deficit of $(201,057,958).

**Governmental funds, June 30, 2022**

| Fund | Revenue | Expenditures | Ending fund balance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| General Fund | $170,116,893 | $172,507,660 | $32,980,837 |
| 2019 Capital Projects Fund | $23,498 | $11,414,598 | $6,840,122 |
| Nonmajor governmental funds | $40,854,075 | $36,192,820 | $10,833,127 |
| Total | $210,994,466 | $220,115,078 | $50,654,086 |

The net change in total governmental fund balances was $(7,190,292) from a beginning balance of $57,844,378. Management reports the General Fund's total available (unassigned) fund balance at 16.6 percent of 2022 general operating expenditures; the board's policy minimum is 15 percent.

**Budget versus actual, General Fund**
Original budgeted revenue of $163,603,984 was amended to $170,565,175 against actual revenue of $170,116,893; original budgeted expenditures of $166,301,381 were amended to $173,657,294 against actual expenditures of $172,507,660. Budgeted revenue was increased $7.0 million, with federal revenue increased $5.0 million for ESSER III and Section 11t American Rescue Plan funding, plus $1.2 million of transfers in from the Community Service and Troy School District Preschool funds.

**Capital assets and debt**
Total capital assets were $400,750,723 less accumulated depreciation and amortization of $201,792,959, or $198,957,764 net. Depreciation and amortization expense was $9,725,109. Construction commitments totaled $8,090,089 spent to date with $8,836,206 remaining. General obligation bonds outstanding were $116,165,000 plus $6,970,844 of unamortized premium; total long-term debt was $131,831,910, of which $17,430,446 is due within one year. The bond rating is AA/Stable, affirmed by Standard & Poor's in May 2021.

**Pension and OPEB (MPSERS)**
Net pension liability $210,869,230 and net OPEB liability $13,509,781, both measured as of September 30, 2021. Pension expense was $25,126,063 and OPEB recovery was $7,228,236. Required and actual contributions were $31,043,947 for pension and $7,221,409 for OPEB.

**Enrollment and outlook**
Spring 2022 enrollment was 12,519 students, roughly 600 fewer than the district was funded for in 2020, equating to approximately $6 million less annual operational revenue. The state foundation allowance rises by $450 to $9,880 per pupil for 2022-2023. A $555 million bond proposal goes to voters on November 8, 2022; if passed, the debt millage is expected to increase by 2.0 mills.
2022_27_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_a.verbose:
Troy School District's Annual Comprehensive Financial Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2022 was presented to the Board of Education as agenda item 8.B on October 18, 2022. Prepared by the Department of Business Services at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (248-823-4000, fax 248-823-4013), it was transmitted October 5, 2022 by Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services (rwest@troy.k12.mi.us, 248.823.4022), and Kandice Moynihan, Director of Finance. Plante & Moran, appointed for 2021-22, issued an unmodified opinion dated October 5, 2022 covering the governmental activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining fund information, plus a Government Auditing Standards report of the same date. No findings or questioned costs were reported for federal awards. ASBO International has awarded the district a Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for fiscal years ended June 30, 1989 through 2021, the 2021 certificate signed by President William A. Sutter and Executive Director David J. Lewis.

Board of Education: Karl Schmidt (President), Dr. Nicole Wilson (Vice President), Gary Hauff (Secretary), and trustees Vital Anne, Steve Gottlieb, Elizabeth Hammond, and Dr. Nancy Philippart. Administration: Superintendent Richard Machesky, Ed.D.; Rick West; Assistant Superintendents Christine DiPilato (Secondary Instruction), Jordan Harris (Employee Services), and Kristine Griffor (Elementary Instruction); and Kerry Birmingham, Director of Communications and Strategic Initiatives.

The district enrolls more than 12,000 students across twelve elementary schools, four middle schools, two traditional and one non-traditional high school, and the East campus of the International Academy. Building inventory totals 448.74 acres and 2,185,181 square feet serving 12,519 students, plus 128.30 acres of vacant property; Troy High School (343,207 square feet, built 1992, 2,101 students) and Athens High School (398,426 square feet, 1974, 1,554 students) are the largest. Thirteen schools hold the National Blue Ribbon Award: Barnard, Bemis, Leonard, Martell, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wass, Wattles, Larson, Boulan Park, Athens, Troy High, and International Academy.

The Statement of Net Position at June 30, 2022 reports cash and cash equivalents of $35,230,239, other receivables of $561,076, due from other governmental units of $26,944,685, inventory of $120,177, prepaid expenses of $812,807, restricted assets of $13,129,507, and capital assets of $3,475,889 not depreciated plus $195,481,875 net of depreciation, for total assets of $275,756,255. Deferred outflows of $65,093,678 comprise $414,288 of deferred charges on bond refunding, $46,666,056 of deferred pension costs, and $18,013,334 of deferred OPEB costs. Liabilities of $382,908,130 include accounts payable of $3,190,370, due to other governmental units of $3,798,115, accrued salaries and wages of $9,503,772, accrued payroll taxes and fringe benefits of $6,664,114, accrued interest of $552,804, unearned revenue of $2,988,034, noncurrent liabilities of $17,430,446 due within one year and $114,401,464 thereafter, net pension liability of $210,869,230, and net OPEB liability of $13,509,781. Deferred inflows of $136,165,518 comprise $13,922,709 of revenue supporting pension contributions made after the measurement date, $70,825,415 of deferred pension cost reductions, and $51,417,394 of deferred OPEB cost reductions. Net position is $82,106,682 net investment in capital assets; restricted $3,333,800 for capital projects, $2,048,648 for Food Service, and $917,494 for debt service; unrestricted $(266,630,339); total deficit $(178,223,715).

Statement of Activities expenses were instruction $102,842,242, support services $67,319,848, athletics $2,222,512, food services $4,355,229, community services $7,238,912, interest $3,036,029, and other debt costs $3,151, totaling $187,017,923, offset by charges for services of $4,858,412 and operating grants of $60,219,352 for net expense of $(121,940,159). General revenue of $144,774,402 included property taxes of $35,621,090 for general purposes, $17,683,639 for debt service, and $4,214,109 for capital projects; unrestricted state aid of $82,313,714; unrestricted federal grants of $47,907; investment earnings of $112,766; net gain on sale and disposal of capital assets of $1,122,207; student activities of $2,866,759; and other of $792,211. Change in net position was $22,834,243 from a beginning deficit of $(201,057,958).

Combined governmental fund balance was $50,654,086, a decrease of $7.2 million per the MD&A, from a beginning balance of $57,844,378. General Fund revenue was $170,116,893 (local $37,421,546; state $111,699,626; federal $10,869,663; interdistrict $10,126,058) against expenditures of $172,507,660, with other financing sources of $2,637,502 including $1,437,502 from sale of capital assets and $1,200,000 of transfers in, for a net change of $246,735 and an ending balance of $32,980,837 (assigned $3,361,479 to the subsequent year's budget; unassigned $28,736,352). Management reports total available fund balance at 16.6 percent of 2022 general operating expenditures against a 15 percent policy minimum, in the seventh consecutive year of adding to fund balance. The 2019 Capital Projects Fund spent $11,414,598 on capital outlay against $23,498 of local revenue and ended at $6,840,122; nonmajor funds ended at $10,833,127, including restricted debt service of $1,470,298 and food service of $1,998,670 and committed community service of $1,709,085 and student activities of $2,145,945. Transfers of $400,000 from the Troy School District Preschool Fund and $800,000 from the Community Service Fund went to the General Fund; $8,411 moved from the Capital Maintenance Fund to the Facility Rentals Fund. Custodial funds ended with net position of $104,643.

General Fund original budgeted revenue of $163,603,984 was amended to $170,565,175 (actual $170,116,893) and expenditures of $166,301,381 to $173,657,294 (actual $172,507,660), with actual basic programs $88,595,157, added needs $24,781,754, pupil support $14,746,569, operations and maintenance $12,115,873, school administration $9,280,734, and instructional staff $9,263,539. Budgeted revenue rose $7.0 million, with federal revenue up $5.0 million for ESSER III and Section 11t American Rescue Plan funding and $1.2 million of transfers in; the final amendment was adopted in June 2022. The Sinking Fund reported $4,220,929 of local revenue and $4,164,977 of capital outlay, ending at $2,787,026.

Gross capital assets of $400,750,723 (land $1,861,010; construction in progress $1,614,879; buildings and improvements $345,755,277; furniture and equipment $50,989,269; building lease asset $530,288) less accumulated depreciation and amortization of $201,792,959 leave $198,957,764 net; additions of $7.8 million covered building renovations, site work, and bus purchases. Depreciation and amortization of $9,725,109 was charged to support services $5,734,528, community services $3,529,994, instruction $242,690, athletics $169,880, and food services $48,017. Construction commitments were $4,089,597 spent with $6,349,512 remaining in the 2019 Capital Projects Fund and $4,000,492 spent with $2,486,694 remaining in the Sinking Fund. Long-term debt moved from $145,880,806 to $131,831,910 with $17,430,446 due within one year; general obligation bonds went from $130,280,000 to $116,165,000 and premiums from $7,678,963 to $6,970,844. Issues outstanding: 2014 $52,710,000 bond, $2,000,000 remaining at 5.00% to May 1, 2023; 2015 $31,930,000 refunding, $12,930,000 at 5.00% to May 1, 2026; 2016 $40,000,000 bond, $31,800,000 at 2.94%-4.50% to May 1, 2032; 2018 $7,125,000 bond, $6,610,000 at 3.00%-3.75% to May 1, 2040; 2019 $22,630,000 bond, $19,175,000 at 5.00% to May 1, 2034; 2020 $6,100,000 bond, $5,390,000 at 2.00% to May 1, 2035; 2021 $7,110,000 refunding, $4,945,000 at 0.30%; and 2021 $33,315,000 refunding, $33,315,000 at 0.30%-1.56% to May 1, 2028. Debt service to maturity totals $116,165,000 of principal plus $21,651,596 of interest, or $137,816,596. The rating is AA/Stable, affirmed by Standard & Poor's in May 2021. The Troy Career Center building lease leaves $422,874 of principal and $42,854 of interest. Bank deposits of $41,417,368 were uninsured and uncollateralized; MILAF holdings were $55,838 in Cash Management and $7,890,866 in MAX Class, both rated AAAm. Coverage runs through commercial insurance and the SET-SEG shared-risk pool.

Under MPSERS, employer pension rates ran 13.73% to 20.14% and OPEB rates 7.23% to 8.09% for October 1, 2021 through September 30, 2022. Required and actual contributions were $31,043,947 for pension, including $13,922,709 of state UAAL stabilization funding, and $7,221,409 for OPEB. Net pension liability was $210,869,230 and net OPEB liability $13,509,781, both measured September 30, 2021 from a September 30, 2020 valuation rolled forward, at a proportion of approximately 0.89 percent. Pension expense was $25,126,063 and OPEB recovery was $7,228,236. Payables to the plans were $6,200,116 and $971,051. Pension discount rates were 6.00% to 6.80% and the OPEB rate 6.95%. RSI schedules show a net pension liability of $308,094,061 for plan year 2020, covered payroll of $79,799,032, and fiduciary net position at 72.32 percent of total pension liability, plus a net OPEB liability of $48,088,931 for 2020 with fiduciary net position at 88.87 percent.

Tax abatements under PA 198 of 1974 and brownfield redevelopment agreements reduced property tax revenue by $126,000, with approximately $108,000 reimbursed by the State of Michigan. Tax year 2021 taxable value was $4,319,004,145 (residential $2,724,884,777; commercial $861,201,980; industrial $237,006,200; personal property $495,911,188) at 26.4658 mills, against estimated actual value of $8,638,008,290. District millage was 3.3878 homestead, 18.0000 non-homestead, 4.1000 debt, and 0.9780 sinking fund. A total levy of $57,806,243 produced current collections of $56,864,080 (98.37 percent) plus $654,758 delinquent, or $57,518,838 (99.50 percent). Somerset Collections led taxpayers at $49,518,400, followed by DTE at $36,077,230. Legal debt margin was $635,850,622 against a $647,850,622 limit, with net debt subject to limit of $12,000,000 (1.85 percent); the MD&A cites qualified debt of $104.2 million. Direct and overlapping debt totaled $144,183,395, including $12,176,370 for the City of Troy, $14,585,276 for Oakland County, and $2,727,048 for Oakland ISD. Population was 86,836, per capita personal income $49,211, unemployment 2.10 percent, and full-time equivalent employees 1,072. Operating indicators list cost per pupil of $13,780, revenue per pupil of $13,589, 850 teaching staff, 11.00 percent qualifying for free/reduced meals, and an average teacher salary of $76,031. William Beaumont Hospital led employers with 2,300 and the Troy School District ranked second with 1,308.

GASB 87 (Leases) was adopted July 1, 2021 with no effect on net position; GASB 96 (SBITAs) takes effect for the year ending June 30, 2023 and GASB 101 (compensated absences) for June 30, 2025. Approximately 65.5 percent of General Fund revenue comes from the foundation allowance and state sources. The per pupil foundation allowance rises $450 to $9,880 for 2022-2023. Spring 2022 enrollment is roughly 600 students below the level funded in 2020, which management equates to approximately $6 million less in annual operational revenue. Voters consider a $555 million bond proposal on November 8, 2022, the first since the 2013 approval, expected to raise the debt millage by 2.0 mills if passed.
